extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, judges, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles governing transfer of patent title: assignments before and after issuance, recording requirements and their effects, the distinction between assignments and licenses, and the effect of bankruptcy or death on patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-issuance assignment as effective assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruments made and recorded in the Patent Office before the patent issues, which request that the patent may issue to the assignee and otherwise evince the intention of the assignor to make the assignee the owner of the legal estate or monopoly, will operate as assignments of the patent under the act of 1836 even if the patent issues in the name of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gaylor v. Wilder: where the invention is perfected and a specification prepared, a recorded assignment requesting issue to the assignee and showing intent that the assignee receive the monopoly will operate as an assignment of the patent interest; this construction aids in quieting titles and avoids requiring a subsequent conveyance. Core requirements: invention perfected/specification prepared; assignment made and recorded before issue; terms indicate intent that monopoly vest in assignee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of written instrument for assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: "That every patent shall be assignable in law ... by any instrument in writing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute requires a written instrument (need not be under seal). To operate as an assignment it must, for the territory it concerns, convey absolutely the exclusive interest vested in the patentee. The statute contemplates assignability as to the whole interest or any undivided part, and also grants of exclusive rights limited to specified parts of the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of conveyances required to be recorded
rubrics_metrics.description: Three classes of conveyances are required to be recorded: (1) assignment of the whole patent; (2) assignment of an undivided part of the patent; and (3) grant or conveyance of the exclusive right to make and use, and to grant to others to make and use, the thing patented within and throughout any specified part or portion of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only instruments that divest the patentee of all interest in the affected part/territory (i.e., vest an exclusive interest) fall within the statutory recording requirement. Instruments that merely grant concurrent or nonexclusive privileges are licenses and need not be recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording within three months — purpose and general effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute requires that assignment, grant, or conveyance shall be recorded in the Patent Office within three months from the date thereof; later statutes add that such conveyance shall be void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee for a valuable consideration, without notice, unless recorded within three months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial construction (Story, McLean) treated the three-month recording requirement as primarily directory to protect bona fide purchasers without notice. The provision enables purchasers to rely on Patent Office records for outstanding titles during that period. Recording within three months protects assignees against subsequent purchasers; failure to record within three months may prejudice the assignee as to intermediate purchasers, but generally does not destroy the assignment as between grantor and grantee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of non-recording against patentee and third persons
rubrics_metrics.description: As against the patentee himself, an assignment vests a good title in the assignee from the time of its execution and recording within three months is not necessary to its validity. As against third persons, an assignee may maintain suit provided he records his title at any time before the trial or hearing. As to subsequent purchasers without notice and for value, the prior assignment must be recorded within three months to prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an assignment is not recorded within three months it is still valid between the parties. A subsequent recording (even after suit commencement) will generally suffice if made before trial. However, a purchaser who purchases in good faith and for value within the three-month window without notice is protected against an unrecorded prior assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment vs license distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: If an instrument vests in the grantee an exclusive interest so that the patentee can exercise no control over that interest, it is an assignment required to be recorded. If it grants a right or privilege to make, vend, or use the subject concurrently with the patentee or other grantees, it is a license and is not required to be recorded by the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on exclusivity: exclusive grants/assignments (whole or undivided/territorial exclusives) are statutory subjects of recording; nonexclusive permissions or concurrent rights are licenses and fall outside the recording regime. Further illustrations and case law are provided in the treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment by operation of law — bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment by act or operation of law is where the title passed without any conveyance by the patentee or other person holding the legal title; for example, where a bankruptcy divests a person of all his property, a patent interest passes with the rest of his estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is certainly true of a patent already issued before the assignment in bankruptcy. In some English cases a patent issued after an act of bankruptcy and assignment by commissioners passed to assignees. But where no application for a patent has been made, courts have expressed doubt whether a bankrupt can be compelled to take steps (oath, application) necessary to vest the patent in another. The effect depends materially on whether the invention was perfected and whether local bankrupt law vests the granted patent in assignees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between property in a patented machine and right to use
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere property in a patented machine, as distinguished from the right to use it, may be transferred (e.g., a sheriff may levy and sell the machine) without subjecting the seller to an infringement action; but the sale of the machine does not necessarily pass the right to use the invention as against an inventor who later obtains a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a tangible embodiment (a built machine) exists, its physical ownership may pass under execution or assignment even before patent application; that does not automatically determine the legal right to make or use the machine if a patent is later obtained by the inventor. The law treats corporeal property and patent privileges separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of assignees in bankruptcy to exercise patent privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been suggested that creditors or assignees in bankruptcy do not acquire any right to use or exercise the patent privilege, but are only entitled to the proceeds of a sale of the patent; however, in principle, if title to a patent is cast upon any person by operation of law for the benefit of third persons, the holder should be able to exercise the patent privileges unless the law under which he acts requires immediate sale and conversion into money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudential or statutory considerations may counsel sale rather than working the patent. The assignee's ability to exercise rights depends on the governing bankrupt law and the policy that may require immediate conversion of assets into money for creditors' benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting of right to take patent in legal representatives of deceased inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §10 of the act of 1836 the right to apply for and obtain the patent is made to devolve on the executor or administrator of a deceased inventor in trust for his heirs or devisees; the oath or affirmation of invention is to be varied accordingly, and the right to take and hold the patent is vested in the executor or administrator 'in as full and ample manner ... as the same was held ... by such person in his lifetime.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provision allows executors/administrators to prosecute patent applications for a perfected invention of a deceased inventor; formalities (oath/affirmation) are adjusted to reflect the representative capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording contracts to convey future inventions has limited notice effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract of sale of a future invention, although in terms an absolute sale, can operate only as a contract to convey and there is no statute that contemplates recording of such conveyances. Recording such contracts will not necessarily operate as notice of title so as to defeat a title made by the inventor to another person after he has perfected the invention and obtained a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a contract for a future, not-yet-existing invention cannot point to an existing patent in the records, a subsequent purchaser is not reasonably bound to investigate such recorded contracts. Such agreements are usually personal covenants enforceable against the inventor, and recording them may in some cases be practically beneficial, but they do not have the same notice effect as recording an assignment of an existing patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: No implied warranty of validity in a mere assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere naked assignment of an interest in a patent, without words which imply an undertaking that the patent is valid, does not import a warranty by the assignor of the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English authorities hold that absent express warranty or equivalent circumstances, a sale/assignment does not carry an implied warranty of title or validity. Parties seeking warranty protection should include explicit warranty language in the conveyance.
